answer: The BFS-vs-DFS comparison in node2vec is relevant because DeepWalk’s random walks are effectively a fixed, unbiased sampling strategy, and node2vec showed that changing the walk bias can matter a lot depending on the graph and task. On sparsely labeled graphs like Flickr and YouTube, the available labels are limited, so performance differences are especially sensitive to whether the embedding method captures local neighborhood similarity (more BFS-like) or broader structural roles/communities (more DFS-like). In practice, DeepWalk’s results on these graphs can be interpreted as evidence that its default walk behavior is closer to a useful BFS-style neighborhood sampler for those datasets, but node2vec also demonstrates that alternative BFS/DFS tradeoffs may improve or change performance. So the comparison is relevant because it helps explain why DeepWalk works well there and whether its success comes from local proximity bias rather than a universally optimal random-walk strategy.
